claim: CD81 belongs to a family of four-pass transmembrane proteins called tetraspanins.
source: CD81 belongs to a poorly understood family of four-pass transmembrane proteins called tetraspanins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a classification of CD81.

claim: CD81 relies on its ectodomain to traffic CD19 to the cell surface.
source: Here, we show that CD81 relies on its ectodomain to traffic CD19 to the cell surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The anti-CD81 antibody 5A6 binds selectively to activated B cells.
source: Moreover, the anti-CD81 antibody 5A6, which binds selectively to activated B cells, recognizes a conformational epitope on CD81 that is masked when CD81 is bound to CD19.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: The 5A6 antibody recognizes a conformational epitope on CD81 that is masked when CD81 is bound to CD19.
source: Moreover, the anti-CD81 antibody 5A6, which binds selectively to activated B cells, recognizes a conformational epitope on CD81 that is masked when CD81 is bound to CD19.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural and binding data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mutations of CD81 in the interface with CD19 suppress its CD19 export activity.
source: Mutations of CD81 in this interface suppress its CD19 export activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 3E.

claim: The CD81-CD19 interaction is dynamically regulated upon B cell activation.
source: These data indicate that the CD81 - CD19 interaction is dynamically regulated upon B cell activation and this dynamism can be exploited to regulate B cell function.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by immunoprecipitation and flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Tetraspanins constitute a 33-member family of transmembrane proteins in humans.
source: The tetraspanins constitute a 33-member family of transmembrane proteins in humans.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Tetraspanins play a critical role in mammalian physiology, functioning in nearly all cell types and regulating distinct processes such as control of cell morphology, cell adhesion, protein trafficking, and signal transduction.
source: Although poorly understood, tetraspanins play a critical role in mammalian physiology, functioning in nearly all cell types and regulating distinct processes such as control of cell morphology, cell adhesion, protein trafficking, and signal transduction (Hemler, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Hemler, 2008.

claim: Tetraspanins achieve their biological functions through interactions with partner proteins, leading to formation of signaling complexes and modulation of signaling activity.
source: Tetraspanins are thought to achieve their biological functions through interactions with partner proteins, leading to formation of signaling complexes and modulation of signaling activity (Hemler, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Hemler, 2005.

claim: Members of the tetraspanin protein family share an overall domain organization consisting of four transmembrane segments, a small extracellular loop (SEL), a large extracellular loop (LEL) containing a conserved Cys-Cys-Gly (CCG) motif, a short cytoplasmic N-terminal region, and a C-terminal cytoplasmic tail.
source: Members of the tetraspanin protein family share an overall domain organization consisting of four transmembrane segments, a small extracellular loop (SEL), a large extracellular loop (LEL) containing a conserved Cys-Cys-Gly (CCG) motif, a short cytoplasmic N-terminal region, and a C-terminal cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about tetraspanin structure in the introduction.

claim: CD81 was discovered as the target of an antiproliferative antibody called '5A6', which inhibits the growth of B cell lymphoma cell lines.
source: CD81, the first tetraspanin identified, was discovered as the target of an antiproliferative antibody called '5A6', which inhibits the growth of B cell lymphoma cell lines (Oren et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Oren et al., 1990.

claim: CD81 plays a critical role in regulating B cell receptor (BCR) signaling as one subunit of the B cell co-receptor complex, which also includes CD19 and CD21.
source: CD81 plays a critical role in regulating B cell receptor (BCR) signaling as one subunit of the B cell co-receptor complex, which also includes CD19 and CD21 (Carter and Barrington, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Carter and Barrington, 2004.

claim: CD81 directly interacts with CD19.
source: Within this complex, CD81 directly interacts with CD19, a single-pass transmembrane protein that establishes the threshold for both BCR dependent and independent signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Stimulation of CD19 lowers the signaling threshold needed for both antigen-independent and antigen-dependent activation of B cells by several orders of magnitude.
source: Stimulation of CD19 lowers the signaling threshold needed for both antigen-independent and antigen-dependent activation of B cells by several orders of magnitude, and this signaling is critical for the function of the humoral immune response (Gauld et al., 2002; Carter and Fearon, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Gauld et al., 2002 and Carter and Fearon, 1992.

claim: Aberrant CD19 signaling is implicated in the development of B cell malignancies, autoimmunity, and immunodeficiency.
source: Not surprisingly, aberrant CD19 signaling is implicated the development of B cell malignancies, autoimmunity, and immunodeficiency (Barrena et al., 2005; Yazawa et al., 2005; Mei et al., 2012; van Zelm et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD19 is the target of chimeric antigen receptor expressing T cells now used clinically in the treatment of B cell malignancies.
source: CD19 is also the target of chimeric antigen receptor expressing T cells now used clinically in the treatment of B cell malignancies (Brentjens et al., 2013; Grupp et al., 2013; Kalos et al., 2011; Kochenderfer et al., 2012; Porter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The association between CD19 and CD81 was first detected using co-immunoprecipitation studies.
source: The association between CD19 and CD81 was first detected using co-immunoprecipiation studies (Bradbury et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Bradbury et al., 1992.

claim: Defects in complex formation between CD19 and CD81 result in severe deficiencies in B cell function.
source: Later, genetic evidence revealed that defects in complex formation between CD19 and CD81 result in severe deficiencies in B cell function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations to mouse studies.

claim: Three independent lines of CD81-null mice showed reduced CD19 surface expression accompanied by defects in B cell function such as weaker early antibody responses, impaired B cell proliferation, and reduced calcium influx following B cell activation.
source: For example, three independent lines of CD81-null mice showed reduced CD19 surface expression accompanied by defects in B cell function such as weaker early antibody responses, impaired B cell proliferation, and reduced calcium influx following B cell activation (Maecker and Levy, 1997; Tsitsikov et al., 1997; Miyazaki et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to three independent studies.

claim: There are human cases of common variable immune deficiency (CVID) in which CD19 expression on B cells is suppressed by homozygous truncations in the CD81 gene.
source: Additionally, there are human cases of common variable immune deficiency (CVID) in which CD19 expression on B cells is suppressed by homozygous truncations in the CD81 gene (van Zelm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to van Zelm et al., 2010.

claim: CD81 is thought to chaperone CD19 through the secretory pathway to the plasma membrane.
source: First, it is thought to chaperone CD19 through the secretory pathway to the plasma membrane (Braig, 2016; Shoham et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a proposed role and supported by citations.

claim: CD81 may serve as a regulator of B cell signaling by controlling the localization of CD19 at the plasma membrane during B cell activation.
source: Second, it may also serve as a regulator of B cell signaling by controlling the localization of CD19 at the plasma membrane during B cell activation (Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a proposed role and supported by a citation to Mattila et al., 2013.

claim: Chimeras that retain the large extracellular loop of CD81 stimulate the same increase in CD19 surface staining as wild type CD81.
source: Chimeras that retain the large extracellular loop of CD81 stimulate the same increase in CD19 surface staining as wild type CD81, but chimeras lacking the large extracellular loop of CD81 do not, indicating that the large extracellular loop is necessary for CD19 surface export.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The large extracellular loop of CD81 is necessary for CD19 surface export.
source: Chimeras that retain the large extracellular loop of CD81 stimulate the same increase in CD19 surface staining as wild type CD81, but chimeras lacking the large extracellular loop of CD81 do not, indicating that the large extracellular loop is necessary for CD19 surface export.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Replacement of the first TM helix of CD81 with that of CD9 or Tspan15 supports the same increase in surface staining as wild type CD81.
source: Replacement of the first TM helix of CD81 with that of CD9 or Tspan15 also supports the same increase in surface staining as wild type CD81, whereas replacement of the first TM helix of CD9 with that of CD81 fails to increase surface staining of CD19, revealing that the first TM helix of CD81 in the context of a CD9 backbone is not sufficient to support the trafficking of CD19 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The first TM helix of CD81 in the context of a CD9 backbone is not sufficient to support the trafficking of CD19.
source: Replacement of the first TM helix of CD81 with that of CD9 or Tspan15 also supports the same increase in surface staining as wild type CD81, whereas replacement of the first TM helix of CD9 with that of CD81 fails to increase surface staining of CD19, revealing that the first TM helix of CD81 in the context of a CD9 backbone is not sufficient to support the trafficking of CD19 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: CD81 exports the CD19/σ1 chimera to the cell surface as effectively as it exports wild-type CD19.
source: CD81 exports the CD19/σ1 chimera to the cell surface as effectively as it exports wild-type CD19, indicating that it is association of the ectodomains that promotes the trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Association of the ectodomains promotes the trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface.
source: CD81 exports the CD19/σ1 chimera to the cell surface as effectively as it exports wild-type CD19, indicating that it is association of the ectodomains that promotes the trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: A secreted form of the CD81 large extracellular loop does not promote increased CD19 surface expression.
source: A secreted form of the CD81 large extracellular loop, however, does not promote increased CD19 surface expression, suggesting that membrane tethering plays an important role in CD19 surface delivery by increasing the effective concentrations of the two proteins for each other (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Membrane tethering plays an important role in CD19 surface delivery by increasing the effective concentrations of the two proteins for each other.
source: A secreted form of the CD81 large extracellular loop, however, does not promote increased CD19 surface expression, suggesting that membrane tethering plays an important role in CD19 surface delivery by increasing the effective concentrations of the two proteins for each other (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The abundance of the CD19-CD81 fusion protein on the cell surface is comparable to that observed when full-length CD19 is co-expressed with wild type CD81.
source: The abundance of the CD19-CD81 fusion protein on the cell surface is comparable to that observed when full-length CD19 is co-expressed with wild type CD81, indicating that CD81 in the fusion protein is functional in trafficking CD19 to the cell surface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: CD81 in the fusion protein is functional in trafficking CD19 to the cell surface.
source: The abundance of the CD19-CD81 fusion protein on the cell surface is comparable to that observed when full-length CD19 is co-expressed with wild type CD81, indicating that CD81 in the fusion protein is functional in trafficking CD19 to the cell surface (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Four different anti-CD19 antibodies recognize the CD19-CD81 fusion protein.
source: Moreover, four different anti-CD19 antibodies recognize the fusion protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as do three anti-CD81 antibodies, providing further evidence that both CD19 and CD81 are properly folded in the context of the fusion protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three anti-CD81 antibodies recognize the CD19-CD81 fusion protein.
source: Moreover, four different anti-CD19 antibodies recognize the fusion protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as do three anti-CD81 antibodies, providing further evidence that both CD19 and CD81 are properly folded in the context of the fusion protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Both CD19 and CD81 are properly folded in the context of the fusion protein.
source: Moreover, four different anti-CD19 antibodies recognize the fusion protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as do three anti-CD81 antibodies, providing further evidence that both CD19 and CD81 are properly folded in the context of the fusion protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by antibody recognition data.

claim: The 5A6 antibody showed significantly decreased binding of the CD19-CD81 fusion protein compared to the other anti-CD81 antibodies.
source: Surprisingly, however, one anti-CD81 antibody, called 5A6 (Levy, 2017; Oren et al., 1990), showed significantly decreased binding of the fusion protein compared to the other anti-CD81 antibodies (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The 5A6 epitope overlaps with the region(s) of CD81 that contact CD19 in the native complex.
source: Although all four antibodies bind the large extracellular loop of CD81, only 5A6 is unable to detect the CD19-CD81 fusion protein, suggesting that its epitope overlaps with the region(s) of CD81 that contact CD19 in the native complex (Nelson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by differential antibody binding data.

claim: The 5A6 antibody cannot be used to pull down the components of CD21/CD19 complex in a B cell line.
source: A prior co-immunoprecipitation experiment also showed that the 5A6 antibody cannot be used to pull down the components of CD21/CD19 complex in a B cell line, providing further evidence the 5A6 epitope is masked by CD19 (Matsumoto et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to Matsumoto et al., 1993.

claim: The 5A6 Fab binds CD81 at an epitope derived almost exclusively from helices C and D.
source: The 5A6 Fab binds CD81 at an epitope derived almost exclusively from helices C and D (Figure 3A,B), burying a total of 1522 Å﻿ (Hemler, 2005) of solvent accessible surface area.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The 5A6 Fab-CD81 binding buries a total of 1522 Å² of solvent accessible surface area.
source: The 5A6 Fab binds CD81 at an epitope derived almost exclusively from helices C and D (Figure 3A,B), burying a total of 1522 Å﻿ (Hemler, 2005) of solvent accessible surface area.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The paratope of 5A6 is derived from all three heavy chain complementarity-determining regions (CDRs; residues 31–35, 50–66, 99–108) and from the first two light light-chain CDRs (residues 24–40 and 55–61).
source: The paratope of 5A6 is derived from all three heavy chain complementarity-determining regions (CDRs; residues 31–35, 50–66, 99–108) and from the first two light light-chain CDRs (residues 24–40 and 55–61).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Helix C of CD81 moves outward by approximately 7 Å in the 5A6-bound structure compared to free full-length CD81.
source: Helix C moves outward by approximately 7 Å, and Helix D unravels almost completely and moves outward by approximately 11 Å, compared to its position in the structure of free full-length CD81.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison in Figure 3D.

claim: Helix D of CD81 unravels almost completely and moves outward by approximately 11 Å in the 5A6-bound structure compared to free full-length CD81.
source: Helix C moves outward by approximately 7 Å, and Helix D unravels almost completely and moves outward by approximately 11 Å, compared to its position in the structure of free full-length CD81.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison in Figure 3D.

claim: The heavy chain of 5A6 inserts its CDR3 loop between helices C and D of CD81.
source: This structural rearrangement occurs because the heavy chain of 5A6 inserts its CDR3 loop between the helices, allowing it to form polar contacts with S179 and N180.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Helices C and D of CD81 form a solvent-exposed, low polarity region in the CD81 large extracellular loop.
source: These two helices form a solvent-exposed, low polarity region in the CD81 large extracellular loop, and evolutionary analysis reveals that this region is highly variable among the different proteins of the tetraspanin family (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by evolutionary analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: The region containing helices C and D is highly variable among the different proteins of the tetraspanin family.
source: These two helices form a solvent-exposed, low polarity region in the CD81 large extracellular loop, and evolutionary analysis reveals that this region is highly variable among the different proteins of the tetraspanin family (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by evolutionary analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations and NMR studies suggest Helix D of CD81 is the most flexible region of the large extracellular loop.
source: Both molecular dynamics simulations and NMR studies suggest the Helix D of CD81 is the most flexible region of the large extracellular loop (Rajesh et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Rajesh et al., 2012 and Schmidt et al., 2016b.

claim: In molecular dynamics simulations, Helices A, B, and E from the large extracellular loop of CD81 retain their alpha helical structure, but Helices C and D are more labile and show a tendency to lose alpha-helicity.
source: In molecular dynamics simulations, Helices A, B, and E from the large extracellular loop of CD81 retain their alpha helical structure, but Helices C and D are more labile and show a tendency to lose alpha-helicity (Schmidt et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2016b.

claim: Mutation of either helix C or D to polyalanine results in decreased trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface.
source: Mutation of either helix C or D to polyalanine results in decreased trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface, strongly suggesting that each helix contributes to CD19-CD81 complex formation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: Each helix (C and D) contributes to CD19-CD81 complex formation.
source: Mutation of either helix C or D to polyalanine results in decreased trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface, strongly suggesting that each helix contributes to CD19-CD81 complex formation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 3E.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy suggests that CD19 may be compartmentalized in the B cell membrane by CD81 to regulate signaling through the BCR.
source: Super-resolution microscopy suggests that CD19 may be compartmentalized in the B cell membrane by CD81 to regulate signaling through the BCR, but the mechanistic details of how CD81 regulates the localization of CD19 remain poorly understood (Mattila et al., 2013; Zuidscherwoude et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Mattila et al., 2013 and Zuidscherwoude et al., 2015.

claim: Anti-BCR antibody treatment resulted in increased CD69 and CD86 at the cell surface when compared with resting cells, confirming activation of the antibody-stimulated cells.
source: Anti-BCR antibody treatment resulted in increased CD69 and CD86 at the cell surface when compared with resting cells, confirming activation of the antibody-stimulated cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: CD19 showed no difference in surface staining between resting and activated cells.
source: CD19 showed no difference in surface staining between resting and activated cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: When surface CD81 is detected using Ab21, there is no difference between resting and activated B cells.
source: When surface CD81 is detected using Ab21 (Nelson et al., 2018), which recognizes both free and complexed CD81, there is no difference between resting and activated B cells (Figure 4B and C), but when CD81 is detected using the 5A6 antibody, which selectively recognizes free CD81, there is a two-fold increase in surface staining on activated B cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: When CD81 is detected using the 5A6 antibody, there is a two-fold increase in surface staining on activated B cells.
source: When surface CD81 is detected using Ab21 (Nelson et al., 2018), which recognizes both free and complexed CD81, there is no difference between resting and activated B cells (Figure 4B and C), but when CD81 is detected using the 5A6 antibody, which selectively recognizes free CD81, there is a two-fold increase in surface staining on activated B cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Western blotting of whole cell lysates from resting and activated cells with Ab21 and 5A6 revealed no significant difference in protein levels.
source: Western blotting of whole cell lysates from resting and activated cells with Ab21 and 5A6 revealed no significant difference in protein levels, indicating that the increase in CD81 surface staining is not due to increased production of CD81 in activated B cells (Figure 4D) but instead reflects a change in the accessibility of the 5A6 epitope.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in CD81 surface staining is not due to increased production of CD81 in activated B cells.
source: Western blotting of whole cell lysates from resting and activated cells with Ab21 and 5A6 revealed no significant difference in protein levels, indicating that the increase in CD81 surface staining is not due to increased production of CD81 in activated B cells (Figure 4D) but instead reflects a change in the accessibility of the 5A6 epitope.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in 5A6 binding reflects a change in the accessibility of the 5A6 epitope.
source: Western blotting of whole cell lysates from resting and activated cells with Ab21 and 5A6 revealed no significant difference in protein levels, indicating that the increase in CD81 surface staining is not due to increased production of CD81 in activated B cells (Figure 4D) but instead reflects a change in the accessibility of the 5A6 epitope.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of CD19 recovered much more CD81 from resting B cells than it did from activated B cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of CD19 recovered much more CD81 from resting B cells than it did from activated B cells, indicating that the CD19-CD81 complex dissociates in activated B cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E.

claim: The CD19-CD81 complex dissociates in activated B cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of CD19 recovered much more CD81 from resting B cells than it did from activated B cells, indicating that the CD19-CD81 complex dissociates in activated B cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E.

claim: The structure of the 5A6 Fab in complex with the large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD81 was determined to 2.4 Å resolution using x-ray crystallography.
source: To gain insight into the molecular basis underlying the unique reactivity of the 5A6 antibody, we determined the structure of the 5A6 Fab in complex with the large extracellular loop (LEL) of CD81 to 2.4 Å resolution using x-ray crystallography (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The ectodomains of CD19 and CD81 interact dynamically during B cell co-receptor trafficking and signaling upon B cell activation.
source: Our studies show that the ectodomains of CD19 and CD81 interact dynamically during B cell co-receptor trafficking and signaling upon B cell activation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The association between CD19 and CD81 is dynamic and CD19 dissociates from CD81 after B cell activation.
source: Using immunoprecipitation and flow cytometry, we found that the association between CD19 and CD81 is dynamic and that CD19 dissociates from CD81 after B cell activation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The 5A6 antibody has recently shown promise as a therapeutic lead, since it can selectively target malignant B cells while sparing normal cells.
source: Indeed, the 5A6 antibody itself has recently shown promise as a therapeutic lead, since it can selectively target malignant B cells while sparing normal cells (Vences-Catalán et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Vences-Catalán et al., 2019.

claim: In resting B cells, the mobility of a large proportion of CD19 is very low, while in CD81-deficient B cells CD19 diffusion shifts strongly to a faster moving population.
source: For example, super resolution microscopy has shown that in resting B cells, the mobility of a large proportion of CD19 is very low, while in CD81-deficient B cells CD19 diffusion shifts strongly to a faster moving population (Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Mattila et al., 2013.

claim: Control of CD19 diffusion by CD81 could allow regulation of CD19's interaction with the BCR, for example, to prevent high-level constitutive signaling.
source: This control of CD19 diffusion by CD81 could allow regulation of CD19's interaction with the BCR, for example, to prevent high-level constitutive signaling (Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation and supported by a citation to Mattila et al., 2013.

claim: Upon B cell activation, dissociation of the CD19-CD81 complex allows CD19 to freely diffuse in the membrane and interact with the BCR, leading to amplified signaling through the BCR and activation of the B cell.
source: One possible explanation for our data is that, upon B cell activation, dissociation of the CD19-CD81 complex allows CD19 to freely diffuse in the membrane and interact with the BCR, leading to amplified signaling through the BCR and activation of the B cell (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Proximity ligation experiments have shown that CD19 is in close association with the BCR on activated cells when stimulated through IgM.
source: Consistent with this idea, proximity ligation experiments have also shown that CD19 is in close association with the BCR on activated cells when stimulated through IgM (Kläsener et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Kläsener et al., 2014.

claim: CD81 redistributes to the immune synapse of activated B cells.
source: For example, others have shown that CD81 redistributes to the immune synapse of activated B cells (Mittelbrunn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Mittelbrunn et al., 2002.

claim: Several integrins have been reported to associate with CD81 and are involved in CD81-mediated adhesion in the immune synapse in activated B cells as well as in B cell trafficking to lymphoid organs.
source: Several integrins have been reported to associate with CD81 and are involved in CD81-mediated adhesion in the immune synapse in activated B cells as well as in B cell trafficking to lymphoid organs (Levy et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Levy et al., 1998.

claim: The transmembrane regions of tetraspanins are highly conserved, but the large extracellular loop varies among family members in both size and sequence.
source: First, the transmembrane regions of tetraspanins are highly conserved, but the large extracellular loop varies among family members in both size and sequence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as background knowledge about tetraspanins.

claim: Within the large extracellular loop, tetraspanins contain a low-polarity hypervariable region that may be involved in tetraspanin binding partner recognition.
source: Sequence analysis reveals that within the large extracellular loop, tetraspanins contain a low-polarity hypervariable region that may be involved in tetraspanin binding partner recognition (Stipp et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Stipp et al., 2003.

claim: Several other tetraspanins and their binding partners, such as ADAM10 and the C8 family of tetraspanins and the tetraspanin CD151 and integrin α3β1, rely on their ectodomains for binding of partner proteins.
source: Additionally, it is known that several other tetraspanins and their binding partners, such ADAM10 and the C8 family of tetraspanins and the tetraspanin CD151 and integrin α3β1, rely on their ectodomains for binding of partner proteins (Noy et al., 2016; Yauch et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to Noy et al., 2016 and Yauch et al., 2000.

claim: Other tetraspanin-partner protein complexes may also be dynamically regulated upon changes in cell state.
source: Like the CD19-CD81 complex, other tetraspanin-partner protein complexes may also be dynamically regulated upon changes in cell state, and conformationally specific antibodies may serve as powerful tools to investigate and control tetraspanin biology.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Conformationally specific antibodies may serve as powerful tools to investigate and control tetraspanin biology.
source: Like the CD19-CD81 complex, other tetraspanin-partner protein complexes may also be dynamically regulated upon changes in cell state, and conformationally specific antibodies may serve as powerful tools to investigate and control tetraspanin biology.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Co-transfection of CD19 with wild-type CD81 results in a two to four-fold enhancement in CD19 surface staining.
source: Whereas cells transfected with CD19 alone only show a small amount of surface staining (Figure 1B and C), co-transfection of CD19 with wild-type CD81 results in a two to four-fold enhancement in CD19 surface staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: A prior study claimed that the first TM helix of CD81 is the main specificity determinant for trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface.
source: Prior studies have suggested that the first TM helix of CD81 is the main specificity determinant for trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface (Shoham et al., 2006), but this claim has also been called into question (Berditchevski and Odintsova, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to Shoham et al., 2006 and Berditchevski and Odintsova, 2007.

claim: The prior claim that the first TM helix of CD81 is the main specificity determinant for trafficking of CD19 has been called into question.
source: Prior studies have suggested that the first TM helix of CD81 is the main specificity determinant for trafficking of CD19 to the cell surface (Shoham et al., 2006), but this claim has also been called into question (Berditchevski and Odintsova, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to Berditchevski and Odintsova, 2007.

claim: The use of the large extracellular loop to bind partner proteins will be a general property of the tetraspanin protein family.
source: Beyond our finding that the ectodomains of CD19 and CD81 interact to control receptor trafficking and localization, there are other lines of evidence suggesting that the use of the large extracellular loop to bind partner proteins will be a general property of the tetraspanin protein family.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.
